title: Treadmills to deadlifts: Why Gen Z are swapping cardio for strength training
content:
When Antonia Duffin, 34, started going to the gym, she wanted to lose weight and tone up.
It became such a big part of her life that she decided to become a personal trainer alongside her day job in operations for a supermarket chain - and now runs her own women's gym in Manchester.
"Some of my clients want to feel stronger, some want to get in shape for a baby and some are struggling with other conditions like endometriosis and want to feel better," she says.
Hybrid training, like Hyrox, which is sociable and competitive, seems to have taken over from running on a treadmill or general cardio on a bike, she explains.
Antonia also notes an appetite for more strength training workouts among younger clients, adding: "I think people are now realising the importance of it - we're preventing osteoporosis and things like that."
Do numbers bear that out? And how are workouts across the UK changing?
According to Sport England, more young adults are going to the gym, using exercise machines and weights to keep fit compared to nine years ago.
"Gyms offer broader types of exercise, like resistance training, which can improve body composition and shape more quickly than aerobic exercise training," explains exercise expert Dr Andrew Scott, from the University of Portsmouth.
He says social media is having an impact too. "Lots of people are largely learning from influencers, suggesting 'I can do it, this is what I did and so can you'."
Student Will Seward, 19, started going to the gym when he was at secondary school because he wanted to "get stronger and build up his physique".
His workouts - usually three a week - have changed over time, from using running machines and exercise bikes initially to more explosive training using weights, to help build athleticism.
"It's had a real impact on my day to day life," he says, "improving my mood and making me feel generally healthier."
Barbells, kettlebells, dumbbells and cable machines are all part of the strength training Antonia offers in her gym space, located in a shipping container.
Recent research suggests doing the recommended two hours of strength training each week may offer many of the same benefits as regular aerobic exercise, such as lowering the risk of dying from heart disease or stroke while also protecting the brain and boosting self-esteem.
These benefits are not the only appeal of exercise though. Many say they feel a sense of connection when exercising with other people.
Dr Hussain Al-Zubaidi, a GP, personal trainer and triathlete, says there is now "an enormous ecosystem" for those who are already active, featuring gyms, running clubs, fitness apps, social media and wearable tech.
How different age groups meet overall exercise targets varies.
Among nearly 2 million participants in Our Future Health - a health and lifestyle questionnaire - younger age groups were more likely to do shorter bursts of vigorous activity every week like fitness classes, aerobics or football.
While running has fallen in popularity overall, it is still the most common form of exercise for young men and women - and in the top two activities for adults overall.
And organised, social running is thriving, with children, 20-somethings and over 50s accounting for a growing share of participants in parkruns, which are free to everyone and have over 1,400 events taking place across the UK every weekend.

title: In Amish country, nurses go door to door to stop deadly spread of measles
content:
For the past few months, nurse Dale Weiser has been making unexpected home visits.
As the state battles the deadliest measles outbreak in recent history, the clinical supervisor drives 30 miles (48.3km), sometimes daily, to a rural corner of Pennsylvania where many Amish people live.
Walking into strangers' homes, Weiser says she tries her best to be respectful and non-intrusive as she vaccinates dozens of family members against the measles, sometimes around the kitchen table.
"A lot of people that I encounter, they don't have health insurance. They don't have a lot of interaction with the health system, and they just haven't seen the need to get these vaccines," said Weiser, who works for the Chester County Health Department.
"When you start talking and you answer their questions, and build that trust, a lot of times they will make a different decision."
The at-home vaccinations are part of the county and state health departments' strategy to encourage immunisations in the county, which includes an Amish community who abstain from many aspects of modern life, including regular contact with the western medical system.
The state health department told the BBC it has administered nearly 4,300 measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccines at pop-up clinics near the epicentre of the outbreak since it began in late April.
But even as health officials see success in their vaccine programmes, the state has reported four deaths from measles complications, marking the most deadly outbreak the US has seen since 1992.
The infections have led to tensions between state and federal health officials, including vaccine-sceptic Health Secretary Robert F Kennedy Jr.
Those politics are back of mind in the Amish community, where people are growing fearful of more deaths as they watch their friends and family fall sick with the disease, which for decades has been eliminated in the US.
"They're not a community that's as easy to reach - we can't just put up a social media post," Weiser said. "They are suffering at the moment, and we're trying to reach out and make connections."
Amish people began coming to the US in the early 1700s, with the first community settling in Lancaster, Pennsylvania. Known as the "Plain People" for the simple clothes they wear, the Amish are a devout Christian community that does not use many forms of technology, relying on horse and buggies instead of cars.
About 90,000 Amish people live in Pennsylvania, with estimates suggesting around only a quarter of Amish people in the Lancaster area have had the MMR vaccine.
There is no particular religious text advising against vaccines, but Amish people do not have regular contact with the western medical system, or have a way to easily travel to appointments, experts said.
"A lot of people who haven't gotten vaccinated, it's not because they have a strong stance against getting vaccinated for measles. It's just that they haven't gotten around to it. It's not convenient," said Braxton Mitchell, a genetic epidemiologist with University of Maryland School of Medicine who runs a research clinic studying the Amish in Lancaster.
Amish people are extremely social, he said, so when the virus hits one church group, it affects everyone who is unvaccinated.
"Measles is rampant in the Amish community," he said. "People are concerned about it."
He added the community has been especially concerned about the dangers to babies; so far two newborns have died of measles complications, as well as an 18-year-old and a 40-year-old woman, according to state officials.
Chester County public health officials did not wait long to launch a response to the growing measles outbreak in their community, which shares a border with Lancaster County, the epicentre of the outbreak.
Jeanne Franklin, the director of the health department, said officials have been using some of the strategies they employed during the Covid pandemic - knocking on doors in the community to let them know about the outbreak and offering private settings, like people's homes, for immunisations.

WHO-IRCH Working Group 2 advances cooperation on herbal medicine quality and standards
WHO convened an online workshop of the International Regulatory Cooperation for Herbal Medicines (WHO-IRCH) Working Group 2 on quality control, standardization and sustainability of herbal medicines on 23 September 2026.
The workshop brought together around 80 participants from 18 WHO-IRCH members to exchange regulatory and technical experience and identify areas for further cooperation. It was organized by the National Institutes for Drug Control (NIDC) of the National Medical Products Administration (NMPA) of China.
The meeting opened with remarks from YU Jiangyong, Deputy Director of the Drug Registration Department of NMPA; XU Miao, Deputy General Director of NIDC; and Dr Sungchol Kim, Chair of WHO-IRCH and WHO Global Traditional Medicine Centre. Dr Kim expressed WHO’s appreciation to NIDC of NMPA for organizing the workshop and highlighted the value of continued international cooperation and knowledge sharing.
"China’s experience and continued engagement offer valuable opportunities for knowledge sharing and international cooperation," Dr Kim said.
Experts discussed practical approaches to herbal medicine quality evaluation, botanical identification, laboratory testing and regulatory oversight. Experiences were shared by regulators and technical experts from Uganda and Sri Lanka, the United States Pharmacopeia and China.
The workshop contributes to implementation of the WHO Global Traditional Medicine Strategy 2025–2034 by supporting Member States to strengthen regulatory capacity, share technical experience and advance appropriate approaches to the quality and safety of herbal medicines. It also complements WHO’s work on internationally relevant standards, including the International Herbal Pharmacopoeia.
The outcomes will inform the continuing work of Working Group 2 and discussions at the 17th WHO-IRCH Annual Meeting on 16–17 December 2026, preceded by workshops of Working Group 1 on safety and regulation of herbal medicines and Working Group 3 on efficacy and intended use of herbal medicines.
WHO also thanked the National Administration of Traditional Chinese Medicine of China for its continued support for WHO’s work in traditional medicine.
